description: OSC 2015 initially widely interpreted as showing low psychological reproducibility. Gilbert et al. (2016) critique narrowed this interpretation by identifying statistical errors.
t0State: OSC 2015 published, widely reported as showing more than half of psychology studies cannot be replicated. Media and scientific community interpreted results as evidence of a replication crisis.
t1State: Gilbert et al. published critique identifying three statistical errors. OSC conceded major point: data do not provide evidence for pessimistic conclusions. Interpretation narrowed: OSC data do not support the claim that reproducibility is low.
oldClaimsThatMustChange: OSC 2015 provides reliable estimate of psychology's overall reproducibility
More than half of psychology studies cannot be replicated (as an unconditional claim)
claimsThatMustRemain: OSC 2015 found 36% of replications had significant results for 100 specific studies
OSC used five different replication metrics
preQuestions: What did OSC 2015 conclude about psychology's reproducibility?
postQuestions: How did Gilbert et al. (2016) change the interpretation of OSC 2015's findings?
forbiddenAfterT1: OSC 2015 proved psychology has low reproducibility (as unconditional claim)
maxAllowedBlastRadius: Interpretation of OSC 2015's conclusions only; does not affect other replication studies

evidence.exactQuote: We show that this article contains three statistical errors and provides no support for such a conclusion.

description: EU Climate Law (2021) specified only 2030 and 2050 targets with obligation to later propose 2040 target. By 2026, a specific 90% reduction target for 2040 was added via amendment.
t0State: EU Climate Law (2021) established binding 55% reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050. Article 4(3) required a future legislative proposal for a 2040 target within six months of first Paris global stocktake.
t1State: Amended EU Climate Law (2026) now includes binding 90% net GHG reduction by 2040. Proposal includes flexibility: 87% domestic + up to 3% international carbon credits. Political pushback from Italy and France.
oldClaimsThatMustChange: EU Climate Law has no 2040 target
EU only has 2030 and 2050 climate targets
claimsThatMustRemain: Original 2021 law established legally binding 2030 target of at least 55% reduction
Original 2021 law required a future 2040 target proposal
preQuestions: What targets did the original EU Climate Law (2021) set?
postQuestions: What 2040 target was added to EU Climate Law and when?
forbiddenAfterT1: The EU has no 2040 climate target
EU's only binding target is the 2030 one
maxAllowedBlastRadius: 2040 target and related provisions only; 2030 and 2050 targets unchanged

evidence.exactQuote: to allow limited use of international carbon credits, under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, starting in 2036.

description: DPC Meta fine (May 2023) created uncertainty about legal basis for EU-US data transfers. EU-US Data Privacy Framework (July 2023) provided a new adequacy decision, but historical pattern of invalidation narrows confidence in permanence.
t0State: DPC fined Meta €1.2B for violating Art 46(1) GDPR. SCCs + supplementary measures found insufficient. No valid adequacy decision existed for US at time of fine.
t1State: EU-US Data Privacy Framework adopted as adequacy decision (July 2023). Third attempt after Safe Harbor (invalidated 2015) and Privacy Shield (invalidated 2020). Privacy advocates signaled potential new challenges.
oldClaimsThatMustChange: There is no legal mechanism for EU-US data transfers (as of May 2023)
claimsThatMustRemain: Meta was fined €1.2B for pre-DPF transfers
SCCs alone cannot remedy inadequate US surveillance law
DPF is the third adequacy framework attempt; first two were invalidated
preQuestions: What was the legal basis for Meta's data transfers in May 2023?
postQuestions: How did the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (July 2023) change the legal landscape?
forbiddenAfterT1: There is no legal mechanism whatsoever for EU-US data transfers
US data protection is now conclusively adequate
maxAllowedBlastRadius: Legal basis for post-July 2023 data transfers only; does not affect pre-DPF liability

evidence.exactQuote: privacy advocates have signaled they may challenge this framework as well
